questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

options.text: Authentication verifies who you are; authorization verifies what you may do
They are two words for the same check
Authentication is client-side; authorization is always in CSS

questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks permissions. You authenticate first, then authorize each sensitive action.

questions.prompt: Which cookie attribute prevents JavaScript from reading the session cookie? Type it.
questions.explanation: httpOnly makes a cookie unreadable to client JavaScript, protecting the session token from XSS theft.

questions.prompt: Which are sound App Router auth practices? Select all that apply.

options.text: Enforce checks in a Data Access Layer near the data
Authorize inside Server Actions and Route Handlers
Rely on a middleware redirect as the only protection
Use httpOnly, secure, sameSite session cookies

questions.explanation: Enforce near the data, authorize in public endpoints, and secure the cookie. Middleware alone is a coarse, bypassable gate.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: Session ID in a cookie mapping to a DB record
Server functions that check auth near data
Optimistic redirect, not the sole guard

questions.explanation: Sessions can be stateless tokens or DB-backed; a DAL centralizes checks; middleware is only an optimistic gate.

items.text: User logs in and the server verifies credentials
The server sets an httpOnly session cookie
On a later request, the DAL reads and verifies the session
If valid, the protected data is returned; otherwise redirect to login

questions.explanation: Login verifies identity and sets a secure cookie; later, the DAL verifies the session before returning protected data.
